title: Ottawa readies ban on fees for moving investment accounts
summary: The federal government has released draft regulations to stop banks from charging fees when a client moves an investment account to a different financial institution.

image.caption: A proposed regulatory change would ban banks from chargings fees for moving investment accounts to other financial institutions. (iStock/Getty Images)

blocks.text: Business
The federal government has released draft regulations to stop banks from charging fees when a client moves an investment account to a different financial institution.
Would benefit lower-income Canadians and smaller financial institutions, expert says
The proposed change would impact registered accounts such as RRSPs, TFSAs and RESPs, as well as non-registered investment accounts at Canadian banks.
Such fees are typically $150 per account, according to a regulatory impact analysis published on Wednesday by the Department of Finance.

While the ban would eliminate the flat administrative fee to transfer an account, it would not waive product-level costs — like trading commissions, early-redemption penalties on GICs, or mutual fund sales fees — if investments are sold or liquidated during a move to a different bank.

If approved, the new regulations would fulfill Ottawa's promise in the 2025 budget to prohibit investment and registered account transfer fees. The government is set to table its latest federal budget on this afternoon.
A department official says a 30-day consultation period on this issue will begin after Saturday.
Fees associated with personal chequing and savings accounts would not be impacted.

Eliminating transfer fees for investment accounts will encourage Canadians to shop around for banks and financial institutions that better match their needs, says Li Zhang, a financial literacy leader and director of social impact at Chartered Professional Accountants of Canada.

"We tend to be [in] life-long, committed relationships with our financial institutions, which has its drawbacks in some ways, because as we grow and move through our financial lives, our needs change," Zhang said.
"What we needed at 15 [years old] is not what we need at 20, is not what we need at 40. And so you need to look at your financial ecosystem to say, 'Am I being supported?'"
Wealthsimple CEO Michael Katchen praised the government's move toward eliminating so-called "exit fees."

The Toronto-based financial technology company has a vested interest in seeing these charges eliminated. Its main product is a popular app offering commission-free trading, automated investing, banking, and tax services.
"This year alone, Canadians have been charged $73 million in exit fees to move their savings to Wealthsimple," Katchen wrote in a LinkedIn post on Wednesday.
"Every financial institution in Canada could decide today to stop charging these junk fees and end this tax on choice. You don't need regulation to do the right thing."
If this happens, Zhang says it will benefit less wealthy Canadians, and the smaller upstart financial institutions that compete with Canada's biggest big banks.

blocks.text: "It will be easier for smaller financial institutions to steal larger institutional clients, because oftentimes, if you have a certain level of net worth, a lot of times the competing or the new … institution will pay for your transfer fees," she said.
It will also benefit lower-income Canadians, "because that $20, that $150, that whatever the case may be, makes a huge difference on Canadians who are really struggling with affordability."

The Canadian Bankers Association (CBA) says it's reviewing the draft regulations, and will work with Ottawa on their potential implementation. The industry group represents more than 60 domestic and foreign banks operating in Canada.
"We believe that reforms should support efficient account transfers across the broader marketplace," CBA spokesperson Nathalie Bergeron said in an email on Thursday.
